# Redact e-mails and phone numbers

`sed -E -f redact.sed` reads text on standard input and writes it back with every e-mail address `LOCAL@DOMAIN` rewritten to `***@DOMAIN` and every phone number of the form `(ddd) ddd-dddd` rewritten to `(XXX) XXX-XXXX`, everything else unchanged. `LOCAL` is one or more of `A-Za-z0-9._+-`; `DOMAIN` consists of labels of `A-Za-z0-9-` separated by dots and ends in a dot plus at least two letters (`a@b.c` is not an address). Several matches per line must all be replaced.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -E -f redact.sed` with this on standard input:

```
mail ann@example.org or call (555) 123-4567
```

prints:

```
mail ***@example.org or call (XXX) XXX-XXXX
```

The tests run `sed -E -f redact.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `redact.sed`: mask the local part of e-mail addresses and the digits of phone numbers in text. The README gives the exact patterns. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# Join continuation lines

`sed -f unwrap.sed` reads text on standard input. Whenever a line ends with a backslash, remove that backslash and the line break after it, as well as the leading blanks (spaces and tabs) of the following line, and repeat for the joined line (several continuations in a row). A last line that ends with a backslash but has no following line stays as it is. Lines without a trailing backslash are printed unchanged.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -f unwrap.sed` with this on standard input:

```
gcc -o app \
    main.c \
    util.c
echo done
```

prints:

```
gcc -o app main.c util.c
echo done
```

The tests run `sed -f unwrap.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `unwrap.sed` which joins shell-style continuation lines (a trailing backslash) into single lines. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# INI section body

`sed -n -f section.sed` reads an INI file on standard input and prints every line that belongs to a section whose header line is exactly `[server]` (all lines after the header up to, not including, the next line that starts with `[`, or to the end of the file), the header itself excluded; comments and blank lines inside the section are printed too. If the section appears several times all bodies are printed in order. Headers like `[servers]` or `[ server ]` are different sections.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -n -f section.sed` with this on standard input:

```
[a]
x=1
[server]
port=80
host=h
[b]
y=2
```

prints:

```
port=80
host=h
```

The tests run `sed -n -f section.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `section.sed`: print the body of the `[server]` section of an INI file. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# Surname first to given first

`sed -E -f swap.sed` rewrites every line of the form `Name: SURNAME, GIVEN` or `Name: SURNAME, GIVEN (TITLE)` into `Name: GIVEN SURNAME` / `Name: GIVEN SURNAME (TITLE)`. `SURNAME` is the text up to the **first** comma (non-empty, so it contains no comma), `GIVEN` is everything after `, ` up to the optional title, which is the last parenthesised group at the very end of the line, preceded by a space. Lines that do not start with `Name: ` or have no comma after a non-empty surname are unchanged.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -E -f swap.sed` with this on standard input:

```
Name: Doe, Jane (Dr)
Name: Roe, Rick
Note: Hello, there
```

prints:

```
Name: Jane Doe (Dr)
Name: Rick Roe
Note: Hello, there
```

The tests run `sed -E -f swap.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `swap.sed` that rewrites `Name: Surname, Given (Title)` lines as `Name: Given Surname (Title)`. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# sed uniq

`sed -f adjacent.sed` prints the standard input with every line removed that is exactly equal to the previous line (so `a a a b a` becomes `a b a`; lines that differ in a trailing space are different). Blank lines are lines too. A final line without trailing newline is handled like any other.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -f adjacent.sed` with this on standard input:

```
a
a
b
b
b
a
```

prints:

```
a
b
a
```

The tests run `sed -f adjacent.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `adjacent.sed`, a sed-only version of `uniq`: drop a line when it is identical to the line just before it. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# Paragraphs on one line

`sed -f paragraphs.sed` reads text on standard input. Paragraphs are separated by one or more empty lines (lines with no characters at all). Each paragraph becomes a single line made of its lines joined with one space (the lines are otherwise unchanged: do not trim them). Every output paragraph is followed by exactly one empty line (so the output ends with an empty line); empty lines at the start of the input and surplus empty lines between paragraphs produce no output. The test inputs end with a newline.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -f paragraphs.sed` with this on standard input:

```
one
two

three
```

prints:

```
one two

three
```

The tests run `sed -f paragraphs.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `paragraphs.sed` that turns every paragraph (a block of consecutive non-empty lines) into one line, words separated by single spaces, and puts one blank line after each. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# Tidy text

`sed -E -f clean.sed` processes standard input as follows: remove leading and trailing whitespace of every line, replace every run of whitespace (blanks and tabs) inside a line by a single space, then collapse any run of blank lines (lines empty after trimming) into one blank line, and delete all blank lines at the very beginning and at the very end of the text. Nothing else changes.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -E -f clean.sed` with this on standard input:

```


  hello    world  



bye
```

prints:

```
hello world

bye
```

The tests run `sed -E -f clean.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `clean.sed` to tidy text: trim every line, squeeze inner blanks, collapse runs of blank lines and drop blank lines at the start and the end. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# Quote CSV fields

`sed -f quote.sed` reads simple comma separated lines (no commas inside fields) and writes each field enclosed in double quotes, a double quote inside a field doubled: `he said "hi",x` becomes `"he said ""hi""","x"`. Empty fields become `""`, and so does an empty line. Whitespace is kept as is.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -f quote.sed` with this on standard input:

```
a,b c,d
```

prints:

```
"a","b c","d"
```

The tests run `sed -f quote.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `quote.sed` to wrap every comma-separated field of every line in double quotes, doubling quotes that are already inside. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

start.README.md:
# Markdown links to plain text

`sed -E -f links.sed` rewrites every inline link `[TEXT](URL)` (`TEXT` and `URL` non-empty, no `]` in the text, no `)` in the url) to `TEXT <URL>`, all occurrences on a line. An image `![ALT](SRC)` (the `[` is directly preceded by `!`) is not a link and stays exactly as written. Anything that does not match the link shape (`[x]`, `[empty]()`, text in brackets followed by a space and parentheses) is untouched.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -E -f links.sed` with this on standard input:

```
see [the docs](https://example.org/docs) now
```

prints:

```
see the docs <https://example.org/docs> now
```

The tests run `sed -E -f links.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `links.sed` converting Markdown links `[text](url)` to `text <url>` but leaving images (`![alt](src)`) alone. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# sed tail

`sed -f tail3.sed` prints the last three lines of standard input (all of them if there are fewer than three), like `tail -n 3`, without reading the whole input into memory at once (a sliding window); a final line without trailing newline stays without one, as GNU sed does.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -f tail3.sed` with this on standard input:

```
1
2
3
4
5
```

prints:

```
3
4
5
```

The tests run `sed -f tail3.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `tail3.sed`: print only the last three lines of the input, using sed alone. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.

# Rename an identifier

`sed -f rename.sed` replaces every occurrence of `old_name` that is a whole word by `new_name`; `old_name2`, `x_old_name`, `_old_name`, `old_name_` and `OLD_NAME` are other identifiers and stay. A dot, parenthesis or hyphen next to it counts as a word boundary. Everything else is unchanged.

## Example

Starting from these files (a `\n` in a name below stands for a real line break, `\t` for a tab):

```
```

running `sed -f rename.sed` with this on standard input:

```
x = old_name + 1
```

prints:

```
x = new_name + 1
```

The tests run `sed -f rename.sed ...` in a fresh scratch directory, with a minimal environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `TZ=UTC`); only the working directory and the files it contains matter.

prompt: Write `rename.sed` to rename the identifier `old_name` to `new_name` in source text, but only where it is a whole identifier. The tests run GNU sed 4.9.
